I saw it. Mexico is lower than we are, yes, but their book is half the size and much steadier.
So you are saying the ranking is wrong?
Not wrong. Incomplete. We grew faster than every market on that list, and the first three months of a new cohort are always the most volatile.
Fair. What would make the comparison better?
Two more columns. Growth, and the age of the book. With those, the gap between us and Mexico narrows to almost nothing.

Here is the table, and I want to be careful with it, because a ranking always sounds more certain than it is. Mexico has the lowest rate, three point four, and Peru has the highest, seven point eight. Brazil sits in the middle, at four point two. Now, that is the whole story only if the rate is all you care about. Brazil is worse than Mexico on the rate, but it grew faster than any market on this list, nineteen per cent against four, and the book is twice the size. And the fifth market I am not going to use this month. One large customer accounts for most of that rate, which makes it an outlier, and an outlier in a table of five is not a market. It is a mistake waiting to be quoted.

Whenever somebody puts a ranking in front of me, I ask the same first question, and it is not about the numbers. It is this. What is being left out, and who chose the column this is sorted by? Because a ranking looks like a fact and it is a choice. Here is the case I see most often. A large old business and a small new one, side by side, in the same table. The new one will always look worse on a rate, because its customers are young and nothing has settled yet, and it will always look better on growth, because it started from almost nothing. Neither number is a lie. The table is just answering a question nobody asked. And in the meeting, do not argue about the position. That never works, and you sound defensive. Name the two columns that are missing, and offer to add them. Nobody says no to that.

Brazil remains the largest consumer credit market in the region by some distance, with more customers than the next three countries together, but it is not the fastest growing. That title belongs to Colombia this year, where the number of people with a formal credit line rose by nearly a fifth. Interest rates across the region stay far higher than in the United States, and that gap has not narrowed in twenty years, whatever governments have promised. One warning before anybody builds a chart. Each country counts a late payment differently, and each one defines a default at a different number of days. So a small difference between two of these markets means almost nothing, and a big one means less than it looks.
